podcast.title: Birth and Early Life (1964)
podcast.body: Gordon Edgar Downey was born on February 6, 1964, in Amherstville, Ontario, located across Collins Bay from Kingston Proper. His father, also named Edgar, was initially a traveling salesman before transitioning into real estate, while his mother, Lorna, cared for him and his siblings. Gord was the second youngest among his brothers Mike and Patrick, and sisters Charlotte and Paula. "Gordon Edgar Downey was born on February 6, 1964 in Amherstville, Ontario."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Brain Cancer Diagnosis (2015)
podcast.body: In December 2015, Gord Downie experienced his first seizure on a Kingston street, leading to a diagnosis of glioblastoma, an aggressive and incurable form of brain cancer found in his left temporal lobe. "Sometime at December 2015, Gord was on the street in Kingston when the first seizure came on. Something was very wrong. A trip to the doctor resulted in the worst possible news. He had a form of brain cancer called glioblastoma."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Secret Path" Performances (2016)
podcast.body: Following the "Man-Machine Poem" tour, Gord performed a few shows for his "Secret Path" project in Toronto, Ottawa, and Halifax. "After a couple of shows for Secret Path and Toronto Ottawa and Halifax, Gord remained largely out of sight."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Glioblastoma Diagnosis (2016)
podcast.body: In 2016, Gord Downie received a diagnosis of glioblastoma, a terminal form of brain cancer with a grim prognosis of one to five years. "Gordowning was dying. Brain cancer. Something called glioblastoma. The prognosis wasn't good. The condition was terminal. One year, maybe two, five, at best."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Incurable Tumor Announcement (2016)
podcast.body: On May 24, 2016, Dr. James Perry of Sunnybrook Hospital publicly announced that Gord Downie's brain tumor was incurable, news that profoundly shocked Canada. "Good morning. My name is James Perry and I'm the head of the Division of Neurology here at Sunnybrook Hospital. I want to thank you for your attention and your concern in light of the difficult news that you all received this morning. It's my difficult duty today to tell you that Gord Downey's spring tumour is incurable."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lakota Spirit Name and Eagle Feather (2016)
podcast.body: At an Assembly of First Nations gathering in Gatineau in early December 2016, Gord Downie was presented with an eagle feather and given the Lakota spirit name "Omani," meaning "the man who walks among the stars." "He did appear at a gathering of the Assembly of First Nations and Gattanoqua back at early December 2016, where he was presented with an eagle feather, and given a Lakota spirit name, a copy of Omani, the man who walks among the stars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Man Machine Poem Tour (2016)
podcast.body: Following his cancer diagnosis, Gord Downie embarked on the Man Machine Poem Tour with The Tragically Hip, which became a national event and a celebration of his life and the band's legacy. "But that same news conference also announced that the hip was going on tour again, the man machine poem tour. That turned into a national celebration of all things. Gord, all things hip, all things rock, and all things Canadian."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Radiation and Chemotherapy (2016)
podcast.body: Following surgery, Gord underwent 30 rounds of radiation treatment over six weeks, twice a day, five days a week. This was supplemented by an oral chemotherapy drug called Tilosilamide. His brother Pat accompanied him, playing music, including The Bee Gees, during treatments. "After the surgery came 30 rounds of radiation treatment. Twice a day, five days a week for six weeks. He would go in for treatment with his brother Pat who would play music for Gord."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Surgery and Post-Surgical Prognosis (2016)
podcast.body: In early 2016, surgeon Douglas DJ Cook at Kingston General Hospital performed a full temporal lobectomy, removing Gord's left temporal lobe, hippocampus, and additional tissue. The best-case scenario after surgery was 4-5 years without further neurological decline. "His surgeon was Douglas DJ Cook at Kingston General Hospital. Dr. Cook went in and removed Gord's left temporal lobe. This is called a full temporal abectomy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death (2017)
podcast.body: Gord Downie passed away on the night of October 17, 2017, at the age of 53, surrounded by his family, friends, and bandmates. His death plunged Canada into widespread mourning. "Until the morning of October 18th, 2017, when we heard that Gord had died the previous night surrounded by family, friends, and bandmates. He was 53."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death (2017)
podcast.body: Gord Downie passed away on October 18, 2017. His death was met with widespread national mourning, with one poignant tweet summarizing the sentiment as "Canada closed, death in the family." "And when Gord died on October 18, 2017, it seemed like the whole country went into morning."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death (Late October 2017)
podcast.body: Gord Downie died approximately two weeks after Tom Petty's passing in October 2017. His death, though anticipated, was still a shock. "and that was followed two weeks later by the departure of Gord Downey. We knew that one was coming, but when he died, he was still a shock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Death (October 18, 2017)
podcast.body: Gord Downie passed away on the morning of October 18, 2017, triggering an immense and sustained outpouring of national grief and affection across Canada. "And then on the morning of October 18th, we got the news. Gord was gone. The outpouring of affection and grief was immediate and sustained."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Declining Health Rumors (2017)
podcast.body: Throughout the summer and fall of 2017, rumors of Gord's declining health circulated, though no official confirmations were made. "Yet there were rumors of declining health through the summer and the fall of 2017. No one would confirm anything, of course."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Final Public Performance (2017)
podcast.body: On February 2, 2017, Gord Downie made his last public singing appearance at Massey Hall in Toronto, joining Blue Rodeo and opening act The Sadies on stage to perform "Lost Together." "And that would be the last time Gord ever sang in public."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Order of Canada for Indigenous Leadership (2017)
podcast.body: In June 2017, Gord Downie was invested into the Order of Canada, not for his music (as The Hip already held that honor), but specifically for his leadership and advocacy on Indigenous issues. "In June 2017, Gord appeared in Ottawa for investment into the Order of Canada. Not for music, though, because the hip already had an order for that, but for his leadership with Indigenous issues."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Powerful We Day Address (2017)
podcast.body: On July 2, 2017, Gord appeared with Pearl and Daisy Wenjack at We Day in Ottawa, where he delivered a powerful address emphasizing the need for reconciliation and acknowledging the historical injustices of residential schools. "And on July 2nd, Gord appeared in Ottawa with Pearl and Daisy Wengek for We Day, where he gave a powerful address for the need for reconciliation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "11" Signal for Nephew
podcast.body: While preparing for a Saturday Night Live performance, Gord promised his 11-year-old nephew a signal: holding up two index fingers to represent the number 11. This promise consumed his thoughts just before going on stage. "He said, Uncle Gord, can you give me a little signal? And I said, okay, I'll tell you what, I'm going to put my two index fingers up in front of me. You're turning 11 because you're turning 11."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Cactus Relationship" with Band
podcast.body: Gord Downie described his relationship with his bandmates as a "cactus relationship," implying it didn't require much maintenance or "TLC" and thrived in challenging conditions. He believed this approach, with fewer expectations of each other, was healthy for longevity. "Well we have what I like to call a cactus relationship. It doesn't require a lot of water or TLC or anything. And we thrive in extremely dry environments and that's how I think how we do it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Gord Downie Chanie Wenjack Room" on Polaris Prince
podcast.body: The Polaris Prince, a cruise ship navigating the Canadian north, features a dedicated "Gord Downie Chanie Wenjack Room," which serves as a space for conducting "tough and sensitive conversations on the issues of reconciliation." "The Polaris Prince, a cruise ship that applies the Canadian north, has an area called the Gord Downey Cheney Wind Jack Room. This is reserved for holding tough and sensitive conversations on the issues of reconciliation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Advocacy for Indigenous People
podcast.body: Downie was a prominent supporter of Canada's Indigenous people, with his activism dating back to at least 2012 when the band participated in the Great Moon Gathering, an annual educational conference held by Indigenous communities along James Bay. He later helped publicize the horrors of the residential school program, particularly through the story of Chanie Wenjack. His work in this area, including the "Secret Path" project, became a major part of his legacy and quest for reconciliation. "Gord will also be remembered for his work and support of Canada's Indigenous people."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anonymity on the Rink
podcast.body: To enjoy anonymity while playing hockey with friends at an outdoor rink in the east end of Toronto, Gord Downie would dress in his full goalie gear, including his mask, at home before walking to the park. He cherished playing at the "loneliest end of the rink." "Gord would dress in his goalie gear at home including his mask and then walk over to the park, total anonymity. Gord loved it playing there at the loneliest end of the rink."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bill Barilko and the "50-Mission Cap"
podcast.body: The "Fully Completely" album features a song referencing the legend of Bill Barilko's plane crash and the Stanley Cup curse on the Toronto Maple Leafs, bizarrely mentioning a "50-mission cap." This cap, a baseball-type worn by WWII fighter pilots, symbolized a seasoned pilot who had survived at least 50 missions. In the song, Downie uses it as a metaphor for people, like his character, who feign experience by distressing their cap, much like he admits to quoting a hockey card (specifically card #340 from the 1991 NHL Pro Set Hockey Cards about Barilko) to appear more knowledgeable. "Barilco's story is just a metaphor for the image Gord's character in the song wanted to portray."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Brain Cancer Diagnosis and Death
podcast.body: On May 24, 2016, it was announced that Gord Downie had been diagnosed with Gleoblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer. He passed away on the morning of October 17, 2017. Despite the short time remaining after his diagnosis, Downie dedicated his remaining months to tackling issues "so much bigger than him," particularly his advocacy for Indigenous people. "The news of Gord's death came out on the morning of October 17, 2017, because, as we all know, was Gleoblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Brain Reboot for Tour
podcast.body: To prepare for the final tour, Gord basically "rebooted his brain" through intense repetition of 90 songs, aided by written notes and lyrics displayed on a screen. Musical memories, stored in a separate part of the brain, were believed to assist his recovery. "But he powered through, basically rebooting his brain, repetition, repetition, repetition, aided by written notes and lyrics on a screen over and over and over again. 90 songs for the upcoming tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Call to Action to the Prime Minister
podcast.body: During The Tragically Hip's final show on August 20, 2016, in Kingston, Downie directly addressed the then-Prime Minister, who was in attendance, making an urgent demand for him to deal with longstanding problems faced by Indigenous people. "Gord called out the Prime Minister by name who was there, suddenly demanding, okay, not so subtly, that he'd deal with these longstanding problems."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Canadian Thematic References
podcast.body: The longer The Tragically Hip stayed together, the more their music incorporated references to Canadian people, events, and places, making their sound increasingly distinctively Canadian. "the longer the band stayed together the more Canadian their music seemed to be with more and more references to people and events and places."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chanie Wenjack Project - "Secret Path"
podcast.body: With his brother Mike, Downie discovered a February 1967 article in McLean's magazine titled "The Lonely Death of Charlie Wenjak." This article recounted the tragic story of 12-year-old Chanie Wenjack, an Anishinaabe First Nations boy who died of exposure and hunger in October 1966 while attempting to walk 600 kilometers home from the Cecilia Jeffrey Indian Residential School. Downie's "Secret Path" album, graphic novel, and animated film brought Wenjack's story to national and international attention, galvanizing resistance against the residential school system. "This told the story of 12-year-old Cheney Wenjak, a young boy from the Inish Nabi First Nations, who was sent to the Cecilia Jeffrey Indian Residential School in Canora, Ontario."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chanie Wenjack Story as Genesis
podcast.body: The story of Chanie Wenjack, who died trying to walk home from a residential school, was recounted to Gord by his brother Mike after Mike read it in McLean's magazine. This story became the foundational inspiration for Gord's "Secret Path" project. "Mike Downey, Gord's brother, ran across the story in McLean's magazine and told Gord all about it. And that was the genesis of everything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Al Purdy
podcast.body: Downie frequently returned to the work of Canadian poet Al Purdy. In 2002, he appeared in a five-minute short film based on Purdy's poem "At the Quinte Hotel," with Purdy himself also providing a voice. Downie also performed a recitation of the poem during a MuchMusic performance and appeared in a 2015 documentary on Purdy, which included a soundtrack featuring songs and poems inspired by Purdy, to which Downie contributed "The East Wind." "In 2002, Gord appeared in a five minute short film based on the poem."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Crucial Support for The Headstones
podcast.body: His presence and endorsement, alongside Paul Langlois, at The Headstones' showcase gig were pivotal in securing their record deal with MCA. Downie vouched for the band's talent and shared Kingston roots, influencing the label's decision. "The backing of Gordownee and Paul Langwau who were with MC at the time showing up at our, guesswork show at our gas work show. And also the ultrasound show, the showcase... That had just as much to do with us getting signed as our, you know, incredible talent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Death and Public Mourning
podcast.body: Gord Downie died on October 17, 2017, at the age of 53, just weeks shy of the second anniversary of his first seizure. His passing evoked widespread grief, with a poignant tweet at the time capturing the national sentiment: "Canada closed death in the family." "Gord died on October 17, 2017 at the age of 53, just a few weeks shy of the second anniversary of that first seizure."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Encounters with Hugh Dillon
podcast.body: Dillon served as Downie's "light guy" for The Slinks' inaugural high school dance performance. Downie also purchased LSD from Dillon during their high school years. "I was Gordowney's light guy at the first high school dance where his band called the slinks performed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Early Life and Education
podcast.body: Gord Downie was the fourth of five children, born to Edgar (a traveling salesman turned real estate developer) and Lorna, in Amherst View, Ontario, just west of Kingston on the other side of Collins Bay. He attended Kingston Collegiate Vocational High, where former students included Johnny McDonnell, Robertson Davies, and Don Cherry. He later enrolled at Queens University, studying political science and film studies, and developed a deep interest in reading poetry. "Gord was from Amherst View, Ontario, just west of Kingston on the other side of Collins Bay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Enduring Legacy in Reconciliation
podcast.body: Gord Downie's name is expected to be associated with reconciliation efforts for a significant period. His work to foster understanding between Indigenous peoples and other Canadians created a momentum that many hope will continue to grow. "Gord's name will be associated with reconciliation efforts for a long, long time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Engagement with Blues Musicians
podcast.body: Downie frequently attended blues performances at Kingston venues like the Prince George, seeking out and talking with old blues acts such as Luther "Guitar" Johnson backstage. He would also smoke pot with Johnson and his 300-pound drummer, Ola May, in the girls' bathroom, used as a private dressing room. "Me and Gordowney would go to places, downtown in Kingston and watch old blues acts like Luther Guitart Johnson would play at the Prince George."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Enigmatic Song Interpretation
podcast.body: Gord Downie was known for his deep and enigmatic personality, particularly regarding the meaning of his songs. When asked about a song's meaning, he would often reply, "What does it mean to you?", emphasizing that his role was to write the song, and it was up to the listener to interpret it. "I write the song. It's up to you to interpret it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Enrollment in Film Studies
podcast.body: After finishing high school and playing with The Filters, Gord grew tired of performing punky covers and decided to enroll in film studies at Queen's University. It was there that he reconnected with Rob Baker and Gord Sinclair, leading to the formation of The Tragically Hip. "Eventually Gord got tired of playing the punky covers and left to enroll in film studies at Queens, and that's where he ran into Rob Baker and Gord Sinclair again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Environmental Activism
podcast.body: Downie and The Tragically Hip were deeply involved in environmental causes, opposing clear-cutting of old growth forests in BC and advocating for clean water. Downie served as a board member of Lake Ontario Waterkeepers, an organization that fought against companies discharging sewage and planned tire burning (in Bath, Ontario, near The Hip's studio). They also pressed the city of Toronto to explain public beach closures due to pollution. In 2009, Downie and the band formed part of the Swim Drink Fish Music Club, raising funds for clean rivers and lakes. "Gord was a board member of Lake Ontario waterkeepers, which fought to keep the great lakes base and clean."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Experimentation in Vocal Style
podcast.body: Over the course of The Tragically Hip's career, Gord Downie increasingly experimented with different vocal styles and phrasing, contributing to the band's evolving sound. "Gord started experimenting with different vocal styles and phrasing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Family Members
podcast.body: Gord Downie was survived by his four children, his brothers Mike and Pat, and his former partner, Laura-Lee Usher. "Gord left behind four children. His brother's mic had pat. His former partner, Laura Lee Usher, and his four bandmates."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Family and Hockey Influence
podcast.body: Gord's godfather was Harry Sinden, a family friend who later became the coach of Team Canada in the 1972 Canada-Russia series and subsequently worked as coach and general manager for the Boston Bruins. This connection influenced Gord's childhood passion for the Bruins, leading him to wear number four like Bobby Orr, before switching to play goal, a position he thoroughly enjoyed. "His godfather was Harry Sinden, a friend of the family. Harry would later go on to be the coach of Team Canada and the 72 Canada Russia series and then work as coach in GM with the Boston Bruins. And this is why as a kid, Gord was such a Bruins fan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Film Studies at Queen's University
podcast.body: Gord Downie pursued film studies at Queen's University. He was an avid fan of French directors, particularly Francois Truffaut, an influence that manifested in some of The Tragically Hip's music videos. "Gord Downey studied film when he went to Queens University. It was a big fan of French directors like Francois Truffaut, which explains some of the hip's videos."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Future Remembrance
podcast.body: Future plans include exploring Gord Downie's solo career, his activism, poetry, and the story of his final months, alongside the band's journey through the 1990s. "On part two of our remembrance of Gord Downey in the tragically hip, we'll follow the band through the 1990s. And then when we get to the 2000s, we'll veer into Gord's solo world, his activism, his poetry, and ultimately the story of his last months."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Glioblastoma Diagnosis and Seizure
podcast.body: In December 2015, shortly after attending his father's funeral, Gord Downie experienced a seizure while walking down a street in Kingston, Ontario. This event led to a diagnosis of glioblastoma, a very aggressive and incurable form of brain cancer. "In December 2015, shortly after attending his father's funeral, Gord was walking down the street in Kingston, Ontario when he had a seizure."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Harry Sinden as Godfather
podcast.body: Gord Downie's godfather was Harry Sinden, who was the coach and general manager of the Boston Bruins, reflecting Gord's lifelong passion for hockey. "Knowing that Gord was brought into this world with Bruin's coach and GM Harry Sinden as his godfather, and that he was a lifelong hockey fan and player."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: High School Athletics and Music
podcast.body: While attending Kingston Collegiate and Vocational School, Gord attempted basketball but found being in a band to be a much greater priority. He was known to skip games and practices to perform with his groups. "In high school, he tried basketball at Kingston, Collegiate and Vocational School. But by that time being in a band was way more important."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hockey Bloodline (Harry Sinden)
podcast.body: Gord Downie's deep connection to hockey is highlighted by his godfather, Harry Sinden, who is the legendary coach, general manager, and president of the Boston Bruins, as well as the coach for the Canadian team in the 1972 Canada-Russia Series. This family tie is reflected in Downie wearing a Boston Bruins sweater in the "Courage" music video. "Hockey literally runs in the blood of the tragically hip. Well in the veins of Gord Downey anyway. ... That's because his godfather is Harry Sinden, the legendary coach, general manager and president of the Bruins. He was also the coach for the Canadian team in the 72 Canada Rushes series."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hockey Career
podcast.body: As a bantam player, Gord played for Ernestown, located west of Kingston, where he backstopped his team to a provincial B championship. Hockey remained a lifelong part of his identity. "As a bantam, he played for Ernestown, which is just a little further to the West and backstop the team to a provincial B championship."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hockey Goalie and Harry Sinden Connection
podcast.body: Downie was a goalie for Amherst View hockey teams that were good enough to win a provincial title one year. His godfather was Harry Sinden, a Stanley Cup-winning coach for the Boston Bruins and head coach for Team Canada in the 1972 series with the Soviets. This connection, stemming from Sinden's real estate partnership with Downie's father, Edgar, explains why Gord wore number four (Bobby Orr's number) when he played hockey and provided background for The Tragically Hip's song "Fireworks." "His godfather was Harry Sinden, a Stanley Cup winning coach for the Boston Bruins, which explains why Gord wore number four, Bobby Horace's number when he played hockey."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hopefulness in Songwriting
podcast.body: Gord expressed a personal artistic inclination to incorporate a sense of hopefulness into his songs, even when exploring bleak sentiments. He found it challenging at his age and stage to leave a song entirely without a glimmer of positivity, believing listeners would desire some form of eventual resolution or recovery. "It'd be hard for me now at this age and stage to leave a song without a glimmer of hope fullness."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hospitality Towards Interviewers
podcast.body: Gord Downie displayed remarkable hospitality, once arriving early for an interview and offering to go to Starbucks to get drinks for the interviewer. "Gord Downey once showed up to an interview early and he said, that's not a problem. I was just going to Starbucks. Do you want anything?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hugh MacLean Reference in "Fully Completely"
podcast.body: In a track from the 1992 album "Fully Completely," Downie paraphrases a passage from Canadian author Hugh MacLean's 1957 novel, "The Watch That Ends the Night." MacLean, an English professor at McGill, was known for being the first Canadian writer to attempt to describe the national character. Downie picked up the book during The Hip's 1991 "Road Apples" tour, and the referenced passage describes a central character's regret for not proposing to the love of his life due to pride, depression, and mostly a lack of courage. "In the song, Gord paraphrases a passage from MacLean's 1957 novel, The Watch That Ends the Night, a book that he picked up to read between gigs on the road apples tour in 1991."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impact of Death
podcast.body: Gord Downie's passing was listed alongside other prominent musicians whose deaths elicited a strong emotional response from fans, demonstrating the deep connection between artists and their audience. "and Gord Downey."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Indigenous Advocacy
podcast.body: As he aged, Gord Downie deepened his involvement and concern for Canada's Indigenous people, which culminated in the establishment of the Chanie Wenjack Fund, dedicated to reconciliation between First Nations and other Canadians. "And the older he got, the deeper he got into the affairs and concerns of Canada's Indigenous people. This culminated with the establishment of the Cheney-Wenjack fun, a project dedicated to the supported reconciliation between the First Nations of Canada and the rest of us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Indigenous Recognition
podcast.body: On December 6, 2016, Downie was awarded an Eagle Feather at the Assembly of First Nations and was given an honorary Aboriginal name, Wacapi Omane, which means "man who walked amongst the stars" in Lakota. He continued to speak out for Indigenous people, appearing in Ottawa on July 2, 2017. "On December 6, 2016, he was awarded an Eagle Feather at the Assembly of First Nations and given an honorary Aboriginal name, Wacapi Omane, which is Lakota for men who walked amongst the stars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Intensive Treatment and Continued Work
podcast.body: Following his seizure and diagnosis, Gord Downie underwent surgery to remove affected parts of his brain, followed by six weeks of chemotherapy and weeks of rehabilitation. Despite the intensive treatment, he bravely continued to perform, embarking on a final tour with The Tragically Hip and working on his *Secret Path* project, as well as making some solo recordings. "Surgery was required, which involved removing the affected parts of his brain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Kingston Upbringing and Early Connections
podcast.body: Grew up in Kingston, attending high school with Hugh Dillon. He was the frontman for his first band, The Slinks, and later became the iconic singer of The Tragically Hip. "I grew up in Kingston with David Usher and the guys in the hip. We all went to the same high school."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

podcast.title: Live Performance Philosophy
podcast.body: When performing live, Gord described feeling both thrilled and nervous, akin to his initial rehearsals as a teenager. He embraced the improvisational nature of live shows, viewing mistakes or equipment failures as opportunities for spontaneous action, such as twirling a broken mic stand like a baton. "It's very improvisational. But it's sort of, and I like to say that if something goes wrong, it's almost better."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Live Performance Style - Stream-of-Consciousness
podcast.body: During live performances, Gord Downie was characterized by his "weird stream of consciousness tangents." These improvisational and experimental segments were not just entertaining but also fertile ground for new song ideas, with "Nautical Disaster" being an example of a song born from such a tangent. "singer Gord Downey can go off in these weird stream of consciousness tangents. These can be very entertaining, but they're also quite useful for writing new songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Log Cabin Plan with Brother Mike
podcast.body: There was a story that Gord and his brother Mike planned to build a log cabin adjacent to Chanie Wenjack's family home, where Gord intended to spend his final days when his illness progressed significantly. "There was a story that Gord and his brother Mike planned to build a log cabin next door to Cheney Windjaxe family, a place where when he got really, really sick, Gord would live out his final days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lyric Writing Process
podcast.body: Downie carried a notebook filled with fragments of conversations, observations, and ideas. When The Tragically Hip jammed, he would flip through these notes to find lines that resonated with the band's groove and rhythm. He often left the meaning of his lyrics open to personal interpretation, viewing this as a hallmark of a true poet, believing they should be open to all kinds of personal interpretation and pathways to certain truths. "When the band jammed, Gord flipped through these books until he found a line or two that felt really good with what the band was playing in terms of groove and rhythm."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mementos in Rehearsal Space
podcast.body: In The Tragically Hip's rehearsal space at The Bath House, a mic stand used during the band's final gig, a set list from that show, and Gord Downie's boots are preserved, creating a "sacred sort of spot" that symbolizes his enduring presence. "A mic stand from the final tragically-hip gig was standing in Gord Downey's place."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Miraculous Tour Completion
podcast.body: Against all expectations, Gord Downie completed all scheduled shows of the "Man-Machine Poem" tour, and additional dates were even added due to high demand, surprising everyone involved. "But Gord surprised everyone. Not only did he make it through all the scheduled shows unscathed, new shows were added to a comedy demand."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Move to Kingston and Home Sale
podcast.body: After the "Secret Path" shows, Gord largely stayed out of the public eye. His home in the Beaches area of Toronto was sold, and he spent most of his remaining time in Kingston. "His home in the beaches area of Toronto had been sold, and he spent most of his time in Kingston."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Order of Canada Recipient (Post-Diagnosis)
podcast.body: After his diagnosis but before his death, Gord Downie was seen receiving an Order of Canada, an honor that occurred in the period of public "denial" regarding his condition. "his secret path documentary and album showing up to receive an order of Canada."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Philanthropic Work
podcast.body: When not engaged in music, Gord Downie dedicated himself to philanthropic efforts. He served as a board member for Lake Ontario Waterkeeper, an organization focused on protecting the lake and its watershed. "For example, Gordown was a board member of Lake Ontario Waterkeeper, a group devoted to protecting the lake and its watershed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Poet Laureate of Ontario Act
podcast.body: On December 17, 2017, a few weeks after Downie's death, a bill was introduced in the Ontario legislature to create the Poet Laureate of Ontario Act in his memory. Two years later, this bill became law, establishing an official position to carry on Downie's love of poetry. "It was the Poet Laureate of Ontario Act in memory of Gord Dowdy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Poetic Influences and Reading List
podcast.body: Gord Downie deeply engaged with poetry, reading works by Leonard Cohen, Al Purdy, and Irvin Layton. His novel reading list included books by Margaret Atwood and he also read Northrop Frye, a highly influential 20th-century Canadian literary critic. "He also really got into reading poetry. Leonard Cohen, L. Perty, Irvin Layton."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Treatment Cognitive Decline
podcast.body: The cancer and surgery caused significant damage, leading to memory loss (he couldn't remember his children's names), difficulty forming sentences, and general confusion. He resorted to writing reminders on his hands. "Memory loss set in. He couldn't even remember the names of his children. Gord took to writing reminders on his hands. He couldn't form any sentences. There was lots of confusion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Private Memorial
podcast.body: A very private memorial for family and friends was held on October 20, 2017, following Gord's death. "Meanwhile, there was a very, very private memorial for family and friends on October 20th."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Private and Quiet Demeanor
podcast.body: Off stage, Gord Downie remained a quiet and private individual who preferred not to be the center of attention. "Gord remained a quiet private guy who did not want to be the center of attention off stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Resonance of "Tragically Hip" Lyric
podcast.body: During a Saturday Night Live performance of "Grace, Too," Gord Downie became overwhelmed by the line "I'm tragically hip," which resonated so deeply with him that his "inner elevator went from the penthouse to the basement," causing him to forget the subsequent lyrics. "He said I'm tragically hip and it was like, because I just resonated with him and my inner elevator went from the penthouse to the basement. I'd break next speed and I thought I don't even know the next line."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Solo Career Motivation
podcast.body: Despite The Tragically Hip's immense success, Gord Downie felt a creative need to pursue projects outside the band, leading to his solo career. "The hip was a great success but creatively this wasn't enough for Gord. He had things he wanted to do outside the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tour as Therapy
podcast.body: His band, family, and organization indulged Gord's desire to tour, seeing it as a form of therapy to keep him engaged and happy, despite low expectations that he would actually be able to complete it. "If working towards a tour helps him, then let's use that at the very least as therapy to keep him engaged and happy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Treatment Choice
podcast.body: Faced with two grim treatment options—longer life with poor quality of life or a shorter life with better quality of life—Gord chose the latter, prioritizing the ability to accomplish his remaining goals. "Or you can choose to have a shorter time left, but your quality of life will be better during that time. Gord went with option B. That would give him the best chance to accomplish everything he wanted to do in the time he had."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Will to Tour
podcast.body: Despite his severe health challenges and cognitive decline, Gord's incredible will drove him to insist that The Tragically Hip rehearse and tour in spring 2016, even though he couldn't remember song titles, albums, or lyrics. "Gord's will had to have been incredible because he recovered enough through the spring of 2016 to insist that the hip get back together and start rehearsing."

xref.title: Formation (1984)
xref.body: The Tragically Hip was formed in 1984 when Gord Downie reconnected with Rob Baker and Gord Sinclair at Queen's University. They recruited high school student Johnny Fay on drums and a more experienced saxophone player from British Columbia named Davis Manning. "This was 1984."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation and Name Origin (1984)
xref.body: The Tragically Hip formed in 1984 in Kingston, Ontario, with Gord Downie (20 years old at the time), Gord Sinclair, Robbie Baker, Johnny Faye, and sax player Dave Manning (about 15 years older). They took their name from a skit in a 1981 VHS tape called "Elephant Parts," produced by video pioneer Michael Nesmith (formerly of The Monkees). The phrase "tragically hip" also appears in Elvis Costello's 1982 song "Town Cryer" from the "Imperial Bedroom" album. "Things started coming together in 1984 when Gord, then 20 years old, the other Gord, Robbie, Johnny Faye, and a sax player, about 15 years older than everyone named Dave Manning, formed the tragically hip, taking their name from a skit in a 1981 VHS tape making the rounds called Elephant Parts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Lineup Change and Stability (1986)
xref.body: In 1986, the same year Gord Downie graduated from Queens University, founding sax player Dave Manning left the band. He was replaced by Paul Langlois, who had first met Gord Downie in grade 11 and was the son of the school's gym teacher and football coach. With Langlois joining, the lineup of The Tragically Hip remained unchanged for the next 31 years. "In 1986, the same year Gord graduated from Queens with a bachelor's degree, Dave Manning bowed out of the band and he was replaced by Paul Langua, who first met Gord when they were both in grade 11."

xref.title: "Man-Machine Poem" Tour Announcement (2016)
xref.body: Following Gord Downie's diagnosis, The Tragically Hip embarked on the Man Machine Poem Tour in 2016. This tour quickly transformed into a national celebration of Gord, the band, rock music, and Canadian identity. The final show, broadcast on a Saturday night in August, was watched by tens of millions of Canadians, bringing the country to a standstill. "that same news conference also announced that the hip was going on tour again, the man machine poem tour. That turned into a national celebration of all things. Gord, all things hip, all things rock, and all things Canadian. Tens of millions of people stop what they were doing and watch the final show that Saturday night and August."

xref.title: Final Show (August 20, 2016)
xref.body: The band played their final show on August 20, 2016, in Kingston, their hometown. During this concert, Gord Downie notably called out the then-Prime Minister, who was present, to address the longstanding issues facing Canada's Indigenous people. "When the hit played their final show on August 20, 2016 in Kingston, Gord called out the Prime Minister by name who was there, suddenly demanding, okay, not so subtly, that he'd deal with these longstanding problems."

xref.body: In 2016, Gord Downie was diagnosed with glioblastoma, an aggressive and terminal form of brain cancer, with a prognosis of one to five years of survival. "Gordowning was dying. Brain cancer. Something called glioblastoma. The prognosis wasn't good. The condition was terminal. One year, maybe two, five, at best."

xref.title: Canadiana in Music
xref.body: Beginning notably with "Road Apples" and intensifying with "Fully Completely," The Tragically Hip delved deeply into "Canadiana," extensively referencing Canadian places, people, and historical events. This approach was a significant aspect of Gord Downie's lyrical inspiration. xref.title: Deep Hockey Connections
xref.body: The band has a profound love for hockey, with connections running deeper than common knowledge. Gord Downie's godfather is Harry Sinden, the legendary Boston Bruins coach and general manager. Downie wore a Bruins sweater in the "Courage" video, and songs like "50 Mission Cap," "Fireworks," "Lonely End of the Rink," and "Heaven is a Better Place Today" all include hockey themes or references. "To know the tragically hip is to know that they're huge hockey fans. And that love for hockey runs a lot deeper than most people know. ... Hockey literally runs in the blood of the tragically hip. Well in the veins of Gord Downey anyway."

xref.title: Gord Downie's Diverse Inspirations
xref.body: Gord Downie was a well-read individual who drew inspiration for his music and improvisations from a variety of sources, including historical events like the sinking of the Bismarck off the coast of France on May 26, 1941, and popular culture such as the movie Jaws, which was one of his all-time favorites. xref.title: Gord Downie's Enigmatic Nature
xref.body: Gord Downie is described as a deep and enigmatic individual. When asked about the meaning of his songs, his consistent response was, "What does it mean to you?", asserting that his role was to write the song, and it was up to the listener to interpret it. "I mean, I asked him once, what does this song mean? And his answer to all those questions were, what does it mean to you? Well, thanks, Gord, but I didn't write the song. I would, no, no, that's the point. I write the song. It's up to you to interpret it."

"Old blues acts like Luther Guitart Johnson would play at the Prince George."

xref.title: Live Performance Style
xref.body: Live performances frequently featured extended instrumental jams and Gord Downie's lyrical stream-of-consciousness rants. These often involved storytelling, such as the "famous Killer Whale Tank tale," or spontaneous interpolations of other songs, and served as a workshop for developing new material, including songs like "Nautical Disaster" and "Ahead by a Century." "Sometimes he tell a story in the middle of the song, like the famous Killer Whale Tank tale. Sometimes Gord would just go off and start seeing another song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Local Punk Outfit
xref.body: This was a local punk band that Gord Downie encountered, and it notably included Rob Baker and Gord Sinclair, who lived across the street from each other. Despite Gord Downie being a couple of grades behind Baker and Sinclair in school, they expressed a desire for him to join their group at some point. "Eventually he ran into another local band, a punk outfit called Rick and the Rodent S."

xref.title: Medical Support for Final Tour
xref.body: For the "Man-Machine Poem" tour, a dedicated EMS team was hired specifically for Gord Downie, and his surgeon, Dr. Douglas DJ Cook, was present backstage as a precaution due to concerns about seizures from dehydration and sleep deprivation. "A separate EMS team was hired just for Gord to go on tour. Dr. Cook, Gord's surgeon, was in the wings."

xref.title: Past Involvement in Drug Dealing
xref.body: In his youth, Dillon engaged in drug dealing, including selling LSD to Gord Downie and cocaine. At 18, he was trafficking large quantities of marijuana (10 pounds at a time) between Ottawa and Kingston, selling to university students, a path he recognized could lead to prison. "My drug career blew up in my face... I was going 10 pounds a dope at a time and bringing it back to Kingston."

xref.title: Post-Gord Legacy Management
xref.body: Following Gord Downie's passing, the band's legacy requires careful management, as The Hip functions as both a creative entity and a business composed of its remaining four musicians. "Beyond being a band is also a business and a business made up of four other musicians. The hip's legacy will need to be managed."

xref.title: Unexpected Hospitality from Gord Downie
xref.body: Gord Downie once arrived early for an interview and offered to go to Starbucks to get the interviewer a latte, which he did, leaving the interviewer surprised at having "sent Gord Downey out to Starbucks for me." "Gord Downey once showed up to an interview early and he said, that's not a problem. I was just going to Starbucks. Do you want anything? And I was like, yeah, I'll take a lot of things. Okay, I'll be back in a moment and he goes out and I, did I just send Gord Downey out to Starbucks for me?"
